item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_001","answer":"The SCOPe family is b.1.1.4, the immunoglobulin V-set domains, but only the N-terminal domain of CD2 belongs there. The C-terminal domain of CD2 is not another V-set domain; it is an immunoglobulin C2-set domain and belongs to a different Ig family within the same Ig-like beta-sandwich superfamily/fold. So the defensible transfer is the Ig-domain scaffold and broad cell-surface adhesion context, not V-set family membership or the ligand-binding and strand-topology details of the N-terminal CD2 V domain.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_002","answer":"The SCOPe family level that unites cyclin A with transcription factor IIB is the TFIIB-like cyclin family, a.74.1.1. That is a homologous two-cyclin-box repeat family within the cyclin-like fold, and SCOPe treats the relationship as stronger than a generic all-alpha architectural resemblance. The transfer still has limits: the shared family supports the duplicated cyclin-box/helical framework and a remote evolutionary relationship, but it does not make TFIIB a cell-cycle cyclin or justify transferring cyclin A's CDK-binding and cell-cycle regulatory annotations wholesale to TFIIB.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_003","answer":"Xylanase and endoglucanase are in the beta/alpha-barrel fold and belong to the glycosyl hydrolases superfamily, c.1.8. They should not be described as the same close SCOPe family, because SCOPe separates many TIM-barrel glycosidases by family; the shared assignment is at superfamily level. That level is appropriate for a conserved catalytic-barrel framework and evolutionary relationship among glycosyl hydrolases, but substrate specificity and exact active-site loops should be checked directly rather than copied from a xylanase template to an endoglucanase.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_004","answer":"The beta-amylase catalytic domain is in the beta/alpha TIM-barrel fold, in glycosyl hydrolases superfamily c.1.8, but at the SCOPe family level it is a beta-amylase-specific family rather than the same family as soybean beta-amylase unless the representative is itself a beta-amylase chain from soybean. This is a fold/superfamily relationship that supports using a TIM-barrel glycosidase core as a remote template for the catalytic domain; it does not authorize transferring soybean-specific surface features, oligomeric contacts, or every loop around the active site to a generic beta-amylase target.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_005","answer":"This comparison should be stopped at the class/fold distinction: GTP cyclohydrolase I is an alpha+beta enzyme in a distinct tunnel-like fold, whereas cyclodextrin glycosyltransferase/amylase catalytic domains are beta/alpha TIM barrels in the glycosyl hydrolase superfamily c.1.8. A hit to a cyclodextrin glycosyltransferase-like template therefore is not evidence that GTP cyclohydrolase I is a TIM-barrel glycosidase, and glycosyl-hydrolase chemistry must not be transferred onto the GTP-cyclohydrolase enzyme without independent catalytic-site evidence.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_006","answer":"PH domains belong to the beta-sandwich class/fold region of SCOPe, not to the same SCOPe fold as C1 domains. C1 domains are small Zn2+-binding cysteine-rich domains, while PH domains are beta-sandwich phosphoinositide-binding modules. They may co-occur in signaling proteins and protein kinase C architectures, but a PH-domain match is not a C1-domain homolog and cannot transfer C1-specific Zn2+-coordinating cysteines, DAG/phorbol-ester binding, or C1 family membership.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_007","answer":"Bacterioferritin and cytochrome b562 are both all-alpha four-helix-bundle proteins, but they are different SCOPe superfamilies/families inside that broad fold: bacterioferritin is in the ferritin-like diiron-carboxylate lineage, whereas cytochrome b562 is a cytochrome four-helix bundle. The common fold can explain a helical bundle template, but it is too weak to transfer ferritin-like ferroxidase centers, bacterioferritin assembly, or iron-storage function to cytochrome b562.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_008","answer":"A 1gk9 A representative is the Mycobacterium tuberculosis cyclophilin A domain, a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase in the cyclophilin-like fold/family. That makes it a valid template only for a cyclophilin/PPIase-like target, not for the unrelated DNase I-like or other folds that may appear in the same broad all-beta class. The expected function transfer is PPIase/cyclosporin-type cyclophilin chemistry, bounded by conservation of the catalytic pocket.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_009","answer":"The hemerythrin-like family/superfamily is all-alpha and metal-binding, typified by a four-helix bundle with a carboxylate-rich diiron site. It is not the same fold as immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich domains, globins, or TIM barrels, and a hemerythrin representative should only be used to transfer the helical diiron/oxygen-binding framework when the target preserves the metal-ligating residues. It is unsafe to infer Ig-like adhesion, globin heme binding, or beta/alpha-barrel enzyme functions from that assignment.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]},{"question_id":"Q026_010","answer":"Copper nitrite reductase domains are all-beta cupredoxin-like proteins, whereas protein kinases have a different alpha/beta catalytic fold with a nucleotide-binding cleft. A cupredoxin/nitrite-reductase hit therefore does not support protein kinase-like homology or ATP-phosphotransfer chemistry; at most it supports a beta-sandwich/cupredoxin copper-binding domain, and only if the copper-ligating histidines and methionine/cysteine pattern are retained.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}

{"id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","track":"held_out","category":"functional_inference","prompt":"Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?"}

item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","answer":"Canonical serine/threonine/tyrosine protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases are all alpha+beta protein-kinase-like catalytic domains in SCOPe, in fold d.144, superfamily d.144.1. The justified common inference is a homologous or at least very deep kinase-like catalytic core: a two-lobe ATP-binding architecture, phosphate transfer from ATP, and conserved mechanistic features around the nucleotide/Mg2+ and catalytic Asp/Lys-type machinery. The named enzymes should not be collapsed into one narrow family, however: canonical protein kinases phosphorylate protein hydroxyl groups, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases phosphorylate small-molecule antibiotic substrates, and PI3Ks phosphorylate an inositol lipid headgroup. Substrate identity, activation-loop or regulatory-domain control, inhibitor sensitivity, and physiological pathway annotations should therefore be transferred only with external evidence such as conservation of the substrate-binding pocket and regulatory motifs, compatible bound-ligand or mutant structures, biochemical activity data, or release-specific SCOPe family placement showing that the query is in the relevant close family rather than merely the d.144 protein-kinase-like fold/superfamily. A representative chosen from one of the three groups can be a template for the shared catalytic scaffold, but it is unsafe as a direct template for substrate specificity or regulation across those family boundaries.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
